title: A Number That Changed Type on the Way: Casts, Truncation, and What Fits

questions.question: What does static_cast<int>(-2.9) give, and what does static_cast<int>(-2.9 + 0.5) give?
options: -3 and -2, since the cast rounds to the nearest whole number
-3 and -3, since the cast rounds away from zero
-2 and -3, since adding a half moves it further from zero
-2 and -2, since a cast throws the fraction away toward zero and adding a half first does not help below zero
questions.explanation: A cast to int truncates toward zero: -2.9 becomes -2. Adding 0.5 gives -2.4, which truncates to -2. The trick is right for positives only: over 601 values from -3 to 3 it disagreed with correct rounding on 251, all negative.

questions.question: A robot's map has one metre cells, and a position is turned into a cell with static_cast<int>(x). Of twenty positions from -1.0 to 0.9, how many land in cell 0?
options: 10, the ones from 0.0 to 0.9
1, since only 0.0 is exactly zero
19, because everything from -0.9 to 0.9 truncates to 0
20, since every position is within a metre of zero
questions.explanation: The origin cell is twice the size of the others. Measured: 19 in cell 0 and 1 in cell -1 by cast, and 10 and 10 by floor. The cell of -0.5 should be the one below zero, which is what floor_to_int gives.

questions.question: static_cast<int> is applied to nan, to infinity, and to 1e10 on gcc and clang. What did it give?
options: Zero for all three, since an int cannot hold them
-2147483648 for all of them, the same value as a real reading of the most negative int, and it is undefined behaviour
Whatever the platform's maximum is, clamped by the compiler
An exception for nan and the largest int for the other two
questions.explanation: Measured at -O0 and -O2 on both compilers. Not a number, infinity and a number too large are indistinguishable from each other and from a real reading afterwards, which is why the check has to come before the conversion.

questions.question: A timestamp in microseconds is a long long, and is stored into an int. After how long does it first go negative?
options: About 71 minutes, since an int holds 4294967295
About 24 days, since an int counts milliseconds
About 36 minutes, since 2147483647 microseconds is 2147 seconds
Never, since a long long converts safely to an int
questions.explanation: It reads 2147000000 at 2147 seconds and -2146967296 at 2148, which is 35.8 minutes. Converting down is defined by the implementation, so it wraps quietly instead of crashing, and a robot that has been up for 36 minutes has a negative time.

questions.question: Why does IntResult keep ok separate from value, instead of returning a special int when the conversion fails?
options: So that value can be negative
Because every int is a reading some sensor could legitimately produce, so no int can stand for 'it did not fit'
Because the standard requires conversions to return a pair
Because a struct is faster than an int
questions.explanation: A sentinel is a number that now cannot be a result. -2147483648 is exactly the value the raw cast gives for nan, so a sentinel would be the same silent wrong answer under a different name.

questions.question: int x{d} and int y = d are written for a double d. What do the compilers do with each?
options: The braced form is refused on every compiler as a narrowing conversion, and the plain assignment is accepted silently under -Wall -Wextra
Both are accepted, since the fraction is simply dropped
Both are refused, since a double cannot become an int
The plain assignment is refused, and the braced form is accepted
questions.explanation: Brace initialisation is the one place C++ checks whether a conversion loses information, which is what checks/ proves. The plain assignment compiles silently on gcc and clang under -Wall -Wextra, and is reported only by -Wconversion.
